record.original_question: In predator-prey dynamics, does increasing the prey's nutrient supply or carrying capacity genuinely make extinction of both prey and predator more likely, or is that prediction only an artifact of a particular mathematical model? After rewriting a Rosenzweig-type predator-prey system in dimensionless form with the capacity-predation number H = h/b, where h is the half-saturation prey density for predation and b is the prey carrying capacity, does the apparent paradox disappear because increasing carrying capacity b and decreasing half-saturation h both lower the same governing dimensionless quantity and therefore represent the same effect?

evidence.quote: The most important question is whether or not this paradox can be observed experimentally. It is possible that the paradox is purely an artifact of the mathematical models, while in reality increasing the nutrition to the prey never leads to an extinction.
This offers a resolution to the so-called paradox of enrichment.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the Rosenzweig–MacArthur predator–prey system

  dN/dt = r N (1 - N/b) - a N P / (h + N),
  dP/dt = e a N P / (h + N) - m P,

where N(t) ≥ 0 is the prey density, P(t) ≥ 0 is the predator density, and r, b, a, h, e, m are positive constants: r is the prey intrinsic growth rate, b is the prey carrying capacity, a is the maximal predation rate, h is the half-saturation prey density for the Holling type-II functional response, e is the conversion efficiency, and m is the predator mortality.

The classical "paradox of enrichment" asserts that increasing the prey carrying capacity b destabilizes the coexistence equilibrium (via a Hopf bifurcation), so that limit-cycle oscillations of growing amplitude can drive both populations toward extinction.

(a) Rewrite the system in nondimensional form using rescaled time τ = r t and rescaled densities n = N/b, p = a P/(r b), and show that the resulting dynamics depend on b and h only through the single dimensionless capacity-predation number

  H = h / b,

together with the dimensionless parameters γ = e a / r and μ = m / r.

(b) Determine whether, within this nondimensional formulation, increasing the carrying capacity b and decreasing the half-saturation h are mathematically equivalent operations (both decreasing H), and in that sense represent the same biological effect.

(c) On the basis of (a)–(b), decide whether the prediction that increasing the prey's nutrient supply (carrying capacity) makes extinction of both species more likely is a genuine feature of the Rosenzweig–MacArthur framework or merely an artifact of a particular choice of parameters; in particular, address whether nondimensionalization through H = h/b "resolves" the paradox of enrichment.
artifact.status_search_result: The paradox of enrichment is a well-known prediction of Rosenzweig-type models since Rosenzweig (1971); the dimensional-analysis observation that b and h enter only through the ratio H = h/b is straightforward and has been noted in textbook treatments. However, whether this dimensional reformulation truly "resolves" the ecological paradox remains debated: empirical and theoretical work (e.g., Jensen & Ginzburg, Roy & Chattopadhyay, Fussmann et al.) shows the paradox can be mitigated by ratio-dependence, inducible defenses, or spatial structure rather than by rescaling alone. Status is therefore best described as partially solved / debated.

status_evidence.title: Paradox of enrichment - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Several explanations have been proposed including ratio-dependent functional responses and inducible defenses; the paradox remains an active topic of discussion.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple proposed resolutions exist; not settled by a single rescaling argument.
